title: D.B. Cooper: What Did the $5,800 Found on a Riverbank Prove?
description:
In 1971, a man who bought a ticket as Dan Cooper hijacked Flight 305. In 1980, a small part of the ransom was found on the bank of the Columbia River. Follow the ticket, the tie, and one bill examined under a microscope to see how far the physical evidence can take us.

The $5,800 found was 2.9% of the ransom paid. A 2020 study inferred, from one original bill, that immersion in May or June fit the evidence better. The year, the date the bills reached the riverbank, and the hijacker's identity remain unknown. In 2016, the FBI shifted its resources and ended active investigation; it did not announce that the case was solved.

The ticket, tie, and ransom are shown using FBI public-domain archival photos. Other visuals are source-based diagrams and original data cards made from FBI case records and the 2020 study; they are not on-site photographs or original micrographs. See image credits for photo sources and limitations.

chapters.open-counter: A note handed to the attendant

h5v002.text: A man paid cash for a one-way ticket to Seattle.

h5v003.text: The ticket said Dan Cooper. He boarded Flight 305.

h5v004.text: Before takeoff, he even ordered bourbon and soda.

h5v005.text: After takeoff, he handed a note to a flight attendant.

h5v006.text: He then claimed there was a bomb in his briefcase.

h5v007.text: That night, the plane's rear stairs lowered in midair.

h5v008.text: More than eight years later, a boy knelt in sand by the river.

h5v009.text: Later still, agents took a sample from a tie left on the plane.

h5v010.text: Years later, tiny pieces from an original bill went under a microscope.

h5v011.text: What would that note make the people on board do?

h5v012.text: She sat beside him as the note said, eyeing the briefcase.

h5v013.text: She saw wires and red objects inside, but could not verify their power.

h5v014.text: He wore a suit, a white shirt, and a black tie.

h5v015.text: Other passengers sat in the same cabin, unaware.

h5v016.text: She wrote down his demands and sent them to the cockpit.

h5v017.text: His terms were to be met after landing in Seattle.

h5v020.text: They logged the bills' serial numbers before handing them over.

h5v021.text: The FBI heard of the hijacking while the plane was still in the air.

h5v022.text: Ground crews prepared; everyone was still aboard.

h5v023.text: The plane landed in Seattle, and money and parachutes came aboard.

h5v024.text: The money stayed on the plane, but the cabin door opened again.

h5v025.text: Thirty-six passengers were allowed off through that door.

h5v026.text: The hijacker did not leave; he stayed in the emptied cabin.

h5v027.text: Several crew members still had to remain on board.

h5v028.text: The plane had landed. Why would it take off again?

h5v029.text: Because the hijacker ordered the crew to fly on toward Mexico City.

h5v030.text: As night fell, Flight 305 took off again.

h5v031.text: Remember those rear stairs? He jumped from the back of the plane.

h5v032.text: It was after 8 p.m.; no one on the ground could pinpoint where he landed.

h5v033.text: The crew later landed safely, but the man was no longer in the cabin.

h5v034.text: The FBI called the investigation NORJAK, short for Northwest hijacking.

h5v035.text: Agents searched the whole plane for anything he touched or left behind.

h5v036.text: Of the parachutes, he took only two.

h5v037.text: One left-behind chute was missing cords used to tie the ransom bag.

h5v039.text: Media later called him D.B. Cooper.

h5v040.text: That name caught on; it was no proof of identity.

h5v041.text: Flight attendants described the face they saw.

h5v043.text: Why couldn't two descriptions reveal his name?

h5v044.text: Agents wrote down those memories and checked each later suspect against them.

h5v045.text: Leads spread across the U.S.; agents interviewed hundreds of people.

h5v046.text: By the fifth anniversary, agents had considered more than 800 suspects.

h5v047.text: Only 24 had not yet been ruled out. None was confirmed as him.

h5v048.text: Those two descriptions still needed physical evidence to identify someone.

h5v049.text: Even whether he reached the ground alive remained unknown.

h5v050.text: The ground search found no one. What about the ransom?

h5v052.text: Only on February 10, 1980, did that boy find decayed bills in the sand.

h5v054.text: His name was Brian Ingram, and he was only eight.

h5v055.text: He found them at Tena Bar on the Columbia River.

h5v056.text: The serial numbers matched the ransom paid years earlier.

h5v058.text: Remember the $200,000 paid in Seattle? Divide the find by the total.

h5v059.text: That gives 0.029. Convert it to a percentage.

h5v061.text: The rest of the ransom did not turn up with it.

h5v062.text: The numbers identify the source; the sandbar does not reveal the route.

h5v066.text: Aside from the river bills, could the tie identify him?

h5v067.text: In 2001, agents reexamined the tie left on the plane.

h5v069.text: Remember the tie at the start? Agents did obtain a DNA sample.

h5v070.text: The tie was evidence, but the sample's origin still needed checking.

h5v071.text: Identification still needed a reliable sample.

h5v072.text: The tie sample has not yielded a real name in public records.

h5v073.text: Later, Agent Carr thought his odds of surviving the jump were low.

h5v074.text: His view was not based on finding a body.

h5v075.text: On July 8, 2016, investigators shifted resources to other priorities.

h5v076.text: Four days later, it asked holders of new evidence to call.

h5v077.text: It did not announce that the case was solved.

h5v078.text: Some tips only said that someone had suddenly come into money.

h5v079.text: The FBI said that still fell short of proving identity.

h5v080.text: The agency still holds physical evidence from then.

h5v081.text: It singled out cash possibly tied to the ransom.

h5v082.text: It also sought actual parachutes. What can the recovered bill tell us?

h5v084.text: In 2020, Kaye and Meltzer published a study of the riverbank bills.

h5v063.text: The paper compared Tena Bar with the reported jump area.

h5v064.text: The two sites are about 30 kilometers apart.

h5v065.text: That distance does not prove how far the bills drifted.

h5v085.text: The boy who found the money later held this original bill.

h5v086.text: Researchers cut several small pieces from its edge.

h5v087.text: Many pieces, but all came from one bill.

h5v088.text: Remember the microscope? They found diatoms on the bill.

h5v089.text: Diatoms are tiny aquatic algae; different kinds thrive in different seasons.

h5v090.text: The November control bill was briefly soaked in the Columbia River.

h5v091.text: The spring control used river water from Tena Bar.

h5v092.text: Both were later tests, not water from that night.

h5v093.text: The original bill's diatoms differed from those on the control bill.

h5v094.text: Under the microscope, fragments of one broken type stayed clustered.

h5v095.text: River data they cited said this type blooms in late spring.

h5v096.text: Remember that November night? The original bill pointed to another season.

h5v097.text: The authors inferred that May to June immersion fit better.

h5v098.text: Did the bill touch river water before or after it was buried in sand?

h5v099.text: A larger diatom lodged between two bills.

h5v101.text: In a buried-then-flooded control, small algae reached only a few millimeters in.

h5v102.text: Deeper areas had almost no diatoms.

h5v103.text: So this control supports water first, then sand burial.

h5v104.text: Element signals were a qualitative cross-check.

h5v105.text: Some signals neared measurement limits; claims stay narrow.

h5v106.text: The authors said this season-dating method still needs more validation.

h5v107.text: Remember the $5,800 at the sandbar? With no firm date, what does it prove?

h5v109.text: It proves the ransom, not the man.
